extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, prose-writers, orators, and students of rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and recognising the Sublime in poetry and prose: principles, sources, techniques, and common faults that affect lofty or elevated style in literary and oratorical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime consists in a certain loftiness and excellence of language; it does not convince the reason but takes the reader out of himself, acting with an imperious and irresistible force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language that elevates the reader and produces an overpowering, immediate effect rather than merely logical persuasion. A single sublime thought, well timed, can illumine an entire subject; the Sublime is felt rather than argued. Example contrasts: mere reasonable or agreeable prose vs. a passage that 'illumines an entire subject with the vividness of a lightning-flash.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of language (prerequisite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Command of language is the preliminary gift on which all sources of sublimity depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting grand effects, secure mastery of diction, syntax, and vocabulary. Technical facility enables the effective deployment of the five sources of sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of thought (lofty cast of mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain lofty cast of mind or grandeur of conception: sublime thoughts belong to the loftiest minds and are the image of greatness of soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate generous, aspiring thought-life; train the mind toward noble conceptions. This source is primarily natural but can be fostered by study and imitation (examples: Homer, Moses). A naked, simple great thought can itself be sublime (e.g., Homeric moments of silence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigorous and spirited treatment of the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A vigorous and spirited treatment of the passions contributes to sublimity; an appropriate display of genuine passion ('fine madness') is highly conducive to grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sincere, well-timed emotion to raise passages to sublimity; distinguish which passions aid grandeur (vehement, noble passions) from those that are low or merely pathetic. Beware: some passions (pity, grief, fear) are often low and do not always produce sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifice in the employment of figures (figures of thought and speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain artifice in the employment of figures—both figures of thought and figures of speech—helps produce sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate and skillful use of metaphor, simile, and rhetorical figures can elevate language. This is an artful, technical contribution (examples cited throughout from Homer and the great orators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignified expression: proper word choice and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Dignified expression is subdivided into (a) the proper choice of words, and (b) the use of metaphors and other ornaments of diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words that suit the majesty of the thought; use metaphors and ornaments sparingly and fittingly so they enhance rather than distract. Poor word choice or inappropriate ornament weakens sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majesty and elevation of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Majesty and elevation of structure—the overall architecture of the discourse—constitute a principal source of sublimity, embracing and coordinating the other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the whole work so that high passages are supported by an elevated, unified arrangement; sublimity can be structural (grand scale, ascending sequence of points) as much as verbal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and combination of the most striking circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the most striking circumstances involved in what you describe and combine them into one animate, coherent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick vivid, telling details (Sappho, Homer examples) and weld them together without frivolous or unbecoming elements. Reject anything not essential, which produces a 'patched and gaping' effect; concentrate on features that genuinely intensify the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification distinct from sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification gathers together constituent parts and topics to emphasise by repetition and extension; unlike the Sublime (which often consists in a single elevated thought), amplification gives extension as well as grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use amplification when you need extension, peroration, or descriptive breadth, but do not confuse it with sublimity. The orator must usually add sublimity to amplification; styles differ (Demosthenes' abrupt vehemence vs. Cicero's diffusive conflagration) and should be chosen according to purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained universality and lasting effect
rubrics_metrics.description: True sublimity pleases and affects all readers across differences and produces a lasting impression; it is pregnant in suggestion and resists distraction and repeated reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge passages by whether they retain power over time and across audiences: if repeated reading diminishes the effect, it is not truly sublime. Aim for ideas that extend beyond literal expression and lodge in memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and tasteless grandiloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombast is excess that transcends the Sublime and becomes grotesque—affected bulkiness or tasteless grandiloquence diminishes effect and invites ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inflated, hollow, or exaggerated phrasing that seeks grandeur but lacks substance (examples: 'curling torrent flames', 'vomiting to heaven' as becoming burlesque). Strive for genuine elevation rather than loud ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid puerility (over-elaboration) and false sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerility is a pedantic over-elaboration ending in frigidity; false sentiment is an ill-timed or empty display of emotion detached from the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-polish or over-elaborate to the point of frigidity. Avoid gratuitous personal feeling or inflated emotion where the situation does not call for it; such devices leave readers cold and betray narrow minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frigidity and childish absurdities
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity (sterile cleverness or childish conceits) and absurd comparisons degrade style despite occasional flashes of ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject absurd or forced conceits (examples given: odd comparisons in Timaeus, inappropriate personifications) and guard against inventiveness that produces trivial or ludicrous images rather than dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject novelty pursued for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit of novelty and startling originality often produces the faults above (bombast, puerility, frigidity); ornaments which originate in a craving for novelty can be the foundation of failure as much as success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value fitness and weight over mere novelty. Let fresh device arise from genuine need or insight, not from a mere desire to surprise; ornaments should serve substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative emulation of great writers (learning by imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emulous imitation of great poets and prose-writers (Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Thucydides) is a legitimate path to sublimity—an effluence of genius passed from master to imitator—distinct from plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and imitate exemplary passages and forms to internalise lofty patterns of thought and diction; copying well-formed models can inspire sublime effects in those whose natural temper is otherwise cold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques that make language mirror emotion (linguistic mimicry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate syntactic and lexical strategies—e.g., bold combinations of prepositions or constraining diction—can 'torture' language to imitate the agony or anxiety of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linguistic devices that reflect the mental state you depict (Homer's use of opposing prepositions to convey terror) while avoiding affectation; let form echo content to intensify readers' experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate deployment according to genre and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Different occasions call for different forms of sublimity: abrupt, high-strung sublimity is apt for rousing, exaggeration, or violent emotion, whereas diffuse sublimity suits perorations, descriptions, digressions, and historical or scientific treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style to purpose: choose Demosthenes-like vehemence for rousing rhetoric and Cicero-like diffusive breadth when you wish to overwhelm or sustain grandeur over length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against limiting details that reduce peril or grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting qualifying or limiting phrases (e.g., 'one frail timber shields them') can banish terror or grandeur by setting bounds on danger or magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid modifiers that undercut the emotional or imaginative stakes of a passage; preserve the sense of unlimited peril or scope when that is the intent.
